1.why: All screens use a clean sans-serif with visibly widened letter spacing and roomy line height (e.g., the two-line intro on the sign-in screen), though it appears to be a standard system font rather than a dedicated dyslexia typeface.

2.why: Every instruction is in sentence case with no italics and no dense paragraphs; the only all-caps strings are the setup secret and recovery codes, which are data to copy, not instructions to read.

3.why: Each screenshot is a single-column, mobile-width layout with full-width buttons and short lines that wrap comfortably, so content stays readable at phone size.

4.why: Instructions are short and plain (e.g., 'Enter the six-digit code.'), though a few lines are awkwardly phrased, such as 'Enter one unused recovery code. It will be used after it works.'

5.why: Every code field shows the expected format in its placeholder: 'Example: 123456' for six-digit codes and 'Example: ABCD-EFGH-JKLM' for recovery codes.

6.why: The longest text on any screen is a two-sentence intro or status line, so the user is never forced to read a long block to proceed.

7.why: The manual setup secret has a 'Copy setup secret' button and the recovery-code list has 'Copy all codes', so long strings can be copied instead of typed by hand.

8.why: A 'Show QR setup pattern' button reveals a large scannable QR code as an explicit alternative to manual entry, with a note pointing to the manual secret if scanning is difficult.

9.why: Email and codes use standard single HTML input boxes that accept paste and ordinary browser autofill, but the screenshots show no visible autocomplete hints (e.g., one-time-code) to confirm explicit password-manager support.

10.why: Each screen has a clear heading and one standout solid-blue primary button plus a four-segment progress bar, but from step 7 onward all segments are filled so the bar no longer indicates which step the user is on.

11.why: Every screen requests exactly one main action via a single full-width blue button (e.g., 'Send identity code', 'Check code', 'I saved my codes'), with other options clearly secondary.

12.why: Green banners usually state plainly what happened and what comes next ('Identity checked. Next, set up your authenticator.'), but the identity-code confirmation is hedged ('If this identity can be checked, a six-digit demo code is ready.') rather than a direct statement.

13.why: The user can 'Request another code', show/hide the QR pattern, setup secret, and recovery codes, and go back via links, with no warning of penalty for repeating or revealing steps.

14.why: The only error observed, 'Your page check expired. Refresh the page and try again.', names the problem and the fix in plain language without blaming the user.

15.why: No countdown or reading timer appears on any screen and code fields stay open, but the 'page check expired' banner shows a stale-page expiry can interrupt a slow user and forces a refresh.
